name: Pineapple Mint
summary: Pineapple mint is Mentha suaveolens 'Variegata', a cream-variegated, strongly spreading culinary and ornamental mint. RHS and University of Wisconsin–Madison both describe the cultivar but report different mature height ranges; exact dimensions remain unresolved while its suckering habit and need for containment are clear.

identity.guidance: Kew recognizes Mentha suaveolens and describes cultivated Variegata as pineapple mint; RHS names the cultivar and variegated apple-mint aliases. This is distinct from peppermint (Mentha × piperita) and spearmint (M. spicata). Vegetative propagation is the documented route for preserving the named variegated form; no seed-to-true-cultivar claim is made.

growth.short: Suckering perennial with cream-margined, aromatic leaves
growth.guidance: RHS describes a strong-growing colony with softly hairy, apple-scented pale-green leaves margined with cream and small mauve flower spikes. UW–Madison describes soft, crinkled, variegated leaves and shallow rhizomes. Their height descriptions differ (RHS profile range 0.1–0.5 m; UW–Madison 2–3 ft); this source conflict is preserved rather than reduced to one cultivar measurement.

cultivation.short: Moist, well-drained soil; contain the spreading rhizomes
cultivation.guidance: RHS recommends moist but well-drained soil and full or partial sun, and advises restricting the root run in a deep container or choosing a site where spreading is acceptable. UW–Madison says full sun suits cooler climates but shade is useful in hotter climates to prevent leaf scorch. This is regional outdoor/container guidance, not a hydroponic prescription.

flowering.short: Small mauve flower spikes appear in late summer in the RHS context
flowering.guidance: RHS describes tiny mauve flowers in dense spikes in late summer for Mentha suaveolens 'Variegata'. The flowering period is retained as UK garden context, not a universal local calendar.

propagation.short: Divide rhizomes or root spring tip cuttings to preserve the cultivar
propagation.guidance: RHS documents division and planting of rhizomes during the growing season and spring root-tip cuttings. These vegetative routes preserve the named variegated cultivar; seed propagation is not presented as true-to-type.

harvest.short: Mint leaves may be harvested as needed; fresh or dried use is documented
harvest.guidance: UCANR's mint guidance names pineapple mint among mint varieties and says leaves may be harvested at any time for fresh or dried use. This is mint-group practice, not a cultivar-specific regrowth interval or yield promise.

pruning.short: Cut back at season end and remove old woody growth when needed
pruning.guidance: RHS recommends cutting the plant back at the end of the growing season. UW–Madison says removing old woody plants allows new stems to fill in; neither source establishes a fixed pruning height or indoor schedule.

problems.short: Manage spread and monitor for mint pests, rust, and powdery mildew
problems.guidance: RHS warns that the cultivar can become a nuisance if its root run is unrestricted and lists susceptibility to mint beetles, mint moth, sage leafhopper, powdery mildew, and mint rust, especially in dry conditions. UW–Madison also cautions that hot-climate sun can scorch the variegated leaves. These are monitoring cues, not cultivar resistance claims.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The selected sources address soil, outdoor beds, and containers, not nutrient-solution performance.

evidence.note: Both sources describe an extensive, suckering or rhizomatous spread for the named variegated cultivar.

height.reason: RHS gives 0.1–0.5 m while UW–Madison reports 2–3 ft; conflicting regional cultivar ranges are retained in the growth section instead of choosing a single mature-height value.

spread.reason: RHS reports a 1–1.5 m maximum spread while UW–Madison describes width as unlimited; both support containment, but not one universal spread number.

spacing.reason: No universal outdoor spacing or Garden-system position count is established.

evidence.note: Outdoor exposure: RHS permits full or partial sun; UW–Madison adds hot-climate shade to limit leaf scorch. This does not state an indoor grow-light tier.

name: Rau Ram
variety: Species identity; no named cultivar specified
summary: Rau ram is Persicaria odorata, an Asian culinary herb also called Vietnamese coriander. RHS describes its node-rooting stems, distinctive marked leaves, and uncommon temperate flowering; no cultivar or hydroponic recipe is assigned.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Persicaria odorata and lists Polygonum odoratum as a synonym. RHS lists rau ram, Vietnamese coriander and Vietnamese mint among common names. It is not botanical coriander (Coriandrum sativum).

cultivation.guidance: RHS describes a clump-forming plant grown outdoors in summer in rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil and full sun in a sheltered position, with container-under-glass culture for the rest of the year in its UK context. This does not provide controlled-environment nutrient data.

propagation.short: Seed, division, and cuttings are documented
propagation.guidance: RHS lists seed sowing in autumn or spring, division in autumn or spring, and semi-ripe cuttings in summer that root in soil or water. It does not provide a germination-time or temperature value on the reviewed page.

harvest.short: Leaf aroma grows stronger as leaves age
harvest.guidance: RHS describes the aromatic leaves as coriander-like when young and increasingly biting and hot as they age. This gives a useful maturity-related flavor cue but does not establish a fixed harvest interval or yield.

uses.short: Leaves are used in Southeast Asian cooking
uses.guidance: RHS identifies the leaves as used in Southeast Asian cooking and describes their pungent, coriander-like aroma when young, becoming hotter and more biting with age. This is species-level culinary context; the common name Vietnamese coriander does not make it botanical coriander.

growth.short: Spreading perennial with node-rooting stems and marked leaves
growth.guidance: RHS describes Persicaria odorata as a spreading herbaceous perennial about 45 cm tall, with reddish-purple stems and lance-shaped green leaves marked by a dark purple-brown chevron; stems can root at nodes. This is a species-level UK garden description, not a guaranteed indoor footprint.

flowering.short: Small pink flower spikes are uncommon in temperate areas
flowering.guidance: RHS reports tiny pink flower spikes in late summer, but notes they rarely appear in temperate areas. Flowering is a normal development state; the reviewed source does not recommend routine flower removal for this species.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: No selected source establishes this species' hydroponic nutrient requirements or system performance.

evidence.note: RHS describes the species as clump-forming.

height.reason: RHS's height is a species-level UK garden description, not selected as an indoor mature-size value.

spread.reason: No species-specific mature dimensions were selected from the reviewed sources.

spacing.reason: No universal spacing or system position count is established.

light.reason: RHS provides a regional outdoor position but it is not normalized to an indoor grow-light tier or a locally verified exposure class.

name: Bush Nasturtium
variety: Species-level bush nasturtium type; no cultivar specified
summary: Bush nasturtium is Tropaeolum minus, distinct from trailing T. majus and watercress (Nasturtium officinale). Wisconsin Extension describes garden nasturtium leaves and flowers as edible, provides mature-plant care guidance and distinguishes the bush and trailing species; cultivar-specific dimensions remain unassigned.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Tropaeolum minus. Wisconsin Extension distinguishes T. minus as bush nasturtium from trailing T. majus. The common name is not confused with watercress, which belongs to a different family and genus.

growth.short: Bush-type growth; dimensions depend on species and cultivar
growth.guidance: Wisconsin Extension describes garden nasturtiums as either low mounds or trailing plants, and distinguishes bush T. minus from trailing T. majus. Because this entry is species-level and names no cultivar, no single mature height or spread is assigned.

cultivation.short: Lean soil and regular moisture support flowering
cultivation.guidance: Wisconsin Extension advises against routine fertilization except in very poor soil because high fertilizer rates favor foliage over flowers. Nasturtiums tolerate dry soil, but regular watering during growth helps maintain flowering. These are shared garden-nasturtium recommendations, not an indoor or hydroponic recipe for T. minus.

care.short: Remove spent flowers to prolong bloom
care.guidance: Wisconsin Extension reports that deadheading or picking flowers prolongs blooming. Treat this as garden-nasturtium guidance; no cultivar-specific pruning response is established for this species record.

flowering.short: Flowers continue until frost in seasonal garden settings
flowering.guidance: Wisconsin Extension says garden nasturtiums continue blooming until frost. In warm, mild climates they may bloom and set seed year-round and can self-seed enough to become invasive; this seasonal behavior is not a universal indoor flowering calendar.

harvest.short: Leaves and flowers are edible; younger leaves are milder
harvest.guidance: Wisconsin Extension describes nasturtium flowers and leaves as edible and suitable for salads. It reports a peppery, watercress-like flavor, stronger in hotter, sunnier conditions; older leaves may be bitter. These are garden-nasturtium group characteristics, not a flavor trial of every T. minus selection.

problems.short: Watch for aphids and caterpillar feeding; leafminer trails are usually minor
problems.guidance: Wisconsin Extension lists aphids and imported cabbageworm caterpillars among common garden-nasturtium pests. Leafminers may make winding trails in leaves but are reported as causing little damage. Warm-climate self-seeding can also require management; no T. minus-specific resistance is established.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: No source establishes hydroponic compatibility for Tropaeolum minus.

growthHabits.reason: The cultivar/type description is retained in Plant Profile prose; the selected source does not quantify a controlled-vocabulary mature habit for all T. minus.

height.reason: No species-wide dimensions selected; cultivar dimensions should not be generalized.

spread.reason: No species-wide dimensions selected; cultivar dimensions should not be generalized.

spacing.reason: Field spacing is not converted into a Garden position count.

light.reason: Shared garden-nasturtium light advice is not converted into an indoor grow-light tier.

name: Romaine Lettuce
variety: Romaine/cos horticultural type; no cultivar specified
summary: Romaine is a horticultural type within Lactuca sativa, not one named cultivar. Its upright head-forming form and crop-level care are described without assigning a cultivar's dimensions, maturity or heat tolerance.

identity.short: Species identity: Lactuca sativa; romaine/cos type
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Lactuca sativa as cultivated lettuce. Romaine/cos is represented here as a horticultural type; no cultivar is assigned. Red Romaine and named romaine cultivars remain separate identities.

growth.short: A head-forming lettuce type; cultivar dimensions vary
growth.guidance: USU Extension treats cos/romaine as a heading lettuce type and describes its harvest at early heading. This generic identity does not specify a cultivar, final head size, leaf dimensions or mature spread.

cultivation.guidance: UMN Extension notes that lettuce has shallow roots and is sensitive to temperature-related bolting. Keep soil moisture even; interpret Minnesota outdoor dates and field spacing as regional crop guidance only, not indoor schedules or hydroponic pod spacing.

care.short: Watch for moisture swings and tipburn
care.guidance: UMN Extension describes browning leaf margins (tipburn) after a dry spell is followed by renewed watering and growth. Check root-zone moisture consistency before assuming a nutrient deficiency or disease; this is a crop-level warning, not a diagnosis.

harvest.short: Pick leaves or cut a formed head, depending on the type and goal
harvest.guidance: USU Extension describes cos/romaine as harvested in early heading, while general lettuce guidance allows usable leaf harvest and whole-plant cutting. Exact maturity and the choice between repeated leaf picking and whole-head harvest depend on the variety; no cultivar date is assigned to this generic record.

problems.short: Bolting ends the normal leafy harvest window
problems.guidance: UMN Extension reports that heat and long days can trigger bolting in lettuce; leaves may become bitter and the plant stops normal leafy growth. Cultivar-specific heat tolerance and disease resistance remain unknown for this generic romaine type.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: No species-level source selected establishes a universal nutrient-solution response for all romaine types.

growthHabits.reason: No generic dimensions or habit selected for the diverse romaine horticultural group.

height.reason: Cultivar and harvest-stage dimensions vary and are not established here.

spread.reason: Cultivar and harvest-stage dimensions vary and are not established here.

spacing.reason: Field spacing is not a hydroponic position rule.

light.reason: Crop-level outdoor light guidance is not mapped to indoor lamp intensity.

name: Pinguicula 'Weser'
variety: Registered cultivar name; hybrid of P. moranensis × P. ehlersiae
summary: Pinguicula 'Weser' is a registered cultivated hybrid with an RHS-documented rosette, seasonal growth pattern and compact dimensions. RHS care guidance is retained at cultivar scope; no hydroponic or nutrient-solution suitability is established.

metrics.label: RHS maximum height
metrics.note: RHS cultivar profile; not an indoor-system guarantee.

identity.guidance: The Pinguicula naming reference explains the cultivar form and ICPS registration role. A 2026 research paper identifies 'Weser' as registered since 1998 and reports P. ehlersiae × P. moranensis parentage. The name is preserved as a cultivar, not converted into a botanical species.

growth.guidance: RHS describes this as an insectivorous tropical perennial with sticky, pale-green rosette leaves that may flush pink in strong light, plus small pink flowers on upright stems in summer. The cultivar is listed as clump-forming, up to 10 cm tall and 0–10 cm spread.

cultivation.short: Bright filtered light and an open, moisture-aware mix
cultivation.guidance: RHS recommends a light, open potting mix and bright, filtered light. During active growth, it advises sitting the pot in a shallow saucer of rainwater. In winter dormancy, water sparingly without letting the mix dry out, and keep the plant above 5°C (41°F). These are RHS cultivation directions, not a hydroponic protocol.

flowering.guidance: RHS describes small pink flowers on slender, upright stems in summer. No flowering schedule beyond that seasonal description is established here.

propagation.short: RHS lists seed and offset division
propagation.guidance: RHS lists propagation by seed and by division of offsets in late winter. Detailed sowing instructions belong in Seed Profile; this profile does not claim that seed-grown offspring retain the named cultivar identity.

pruning.guidance: RHS states that pruning is not required for this cultivar.

problems.guidance: RHS notes that Pinguicula 'Weser' may be susceptible to slugs and snails and describes it as generally disease-free; that is not a guarantee that disease cannot occur.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: RHS container-care guidance does not establish compatibility with a hydroponic nutrient solution.

evidence.note: RHS describes a clump-forming plant with rosette leaves.
RHS lists maximum height up to 10 cm.
RHS lists 0–0.1 m maximum spread, represented as an approximate 10 cm upper bound.

spacing.reason: No spacing recommendation is selected for the represented indoor/container context.

light.reason: RHS lists full sun or partial shade as positions and recommends bright filtered light; the contract does not encode partial shade without conflating it with partial sun or shade, and this does not establish indoor grow-light intensity.
